core: Context clues defined as the surrounding words and sentences that hint at an unknown word's meaning
Main clue types: restatement/definition, example, synonym, antonym, general-sense — each with an original example sentence
A practical application sequence: read on, look for signal words, check the part of speech, test the guess
Limits of context clues: when guessing fails and looking the word up is the right skill
Context clues vs dictionary use: speed and flow versus exact, verified meaning
Why the skill matters for reading: keeping comprehension moving and meeting new words
supporting: Signal words that announce clue types (which means, such as, however, unlike)
Part of speech as a meaning filter for unknown words
Dictionary lookup and personal vocabulary lists as complements to context
Active reading: noting what you do not understand and rereading
Reading rhetorically: figuring out why and how a message works
outOfScope: Vocabulary-building as intentional word study — separate topic, referenced only
Reading-comprehension strategies at large — separate topic, referenced only
Pronunciation, spelling, and morphology of new words

claims.claim: Context clues are the surrounding words and sentences that help a reader figure out the meaning of an unfamiliar word; strong readers use them rather than stopping at the first unknown term.

A reader can often guess enough of a word's meaning from context to keep reading — for example, a term connected with the work of undertakers and archaeologists can at least be recognized as having something to do with death.
Definitions are among the guides writers place in texts — alongside headings, pull quotes, and tables — that readers can use while reading or skimming.

Looking a word up in a dictionary, online or in print, is a complementary strategy that gives the exact meaning, especially for discipline-specific terms; keeping a personal list of new words supports learning them.
Active reading includes noticing words, phrases, or ideas you do not understand on a first pass and rereading the text to catch what the first pass missed.
Reading to understand and respond involves figuring out why and how a message works, not only decoding its words, so keeping comprehension moving past unknown words matters.

The lesson's framework of clue types — restatement, example, synonym, antonym, and general-sense — is a common classroom way of describing the patterns writers use; every example sentence in the lesson is an original construction demonstrating one pattern.

When the surrounding text offers no usable clues — or the exact meaning matters, as with discipline-specific terms — a dictionary check is the right move; a context-based guess is a hypothesis to test, not a verified meaning.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Teaching sources vary in how many context-clue types they list: some merge synonym and antonym clues, others add cause-and-effect or inference clues.
positions: OpenStax presents context clues and definitions as reading guides without prescribing a fixed type list.
Many classroom frameworks describe four to six distinct clue types.
The five-type list (restatement, example, synonym, antonym, general-sense) is the most common textbook arrangement.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the five-type list as a common classroom framework rather than a canonical taxonomy, and each demonstration sentence is original, so no single source's wording or list is reproduced.

conflictingEvidence.issue: A guess from context is approximate and can mislead when the passage is ambiguous or technical.
positions: OpenStax recommends looking words up in a dictionary to ensure the exact meaning, especially for discipline-specific terms.
About Writing's active-reading guidance asks readers to note what they do not understand and reread.
Reading teachers generally warn that context alone can produce wrong meanings.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches a guess-then-verify habit: use context to form a working meaning, test it against the sentence, and consult a dictionary when precision matters or clues are absent.
